questions.question: A Snowflake layout reserves 12 bits for the per-millisecond sequence. What is the largest number of IDs one generator can issue in one millisecond before it must wait?
questions.explanation: Twelve bits encode 2^12 distinct sequence values: 4,096. Reusing one in the same millisecond would repeat the tuple.

questions.question: Why does placing the timestamp in the most significant data bits make Snowflake IDs roughly sortable?
options: A later millisecond contributes a larger high-order value
It forces every region to serialize requests
It eliminates sequence counters
It makes the sign bit random
questions.explanation: Higher-order timestamp bits dominate the integer value, so IDs from a later healthy-clock millisecond sort after earlier ones.

questions.question: A generator observes a wall-clock time earlier than the last timestamp it emitted. Which response protects uniqueness?
options: Fail the generator closed until time is safe or a defined safe-time policy applies
Reset its sequence to zero and continue
Ask clients to supply a timestamp
Reuse the last ID with a new sign bit
questions.explanation: Moving backward can revisit an already used timestamp, generator-ID, and sequence coordinate. Continuing silently risks a duplicate.

questions.question: What must the machine-identity control plane guarantee while two deployments overlap during a rollout?
options: Only one live, unfenced process owns each generator identity
All generators use the same identity for easier decoding
Every ID request calls the lease service
Sequences are persisted to a database after every ID
questions.explanation: The request path can stay local, but ownership must prevent two live processes from producing the same generator-ID coordinate.

questions.question: What should happen when a generator has consumed every sequence value in the current millisecond?
options: Wait for the next millisecond or shed/reroute load
Wrap sequence to zero immediately
Borrow a machine ID from another generator
Change the custom epoch
questions.explanation: Wrapping inside the same timestamp and generator identity repeats previously issued tuples. Capacity is finite per millisecond.

questions.question: Which workload is the strongest fit for a Snowflake-style 64-bit ID rather than a database sequence?
options: Many independent writers need compact, roughly time-ordered IDs with no database call per ID
One database already owns every authoritative write and strict serial order is required
IDs must be cryptographically unguessable public secrets
Only random string identifiers are supported
questions.explanation: Snowflake-style IDs trade request-time coordination for disciplined clocks and identity leases, making them useful for many low-latency writers.
